messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Harjit Singh is an 80-year-old widowed Coast Guard veteran who came to treatment after many years of living inside an event he still struggles to describe in a straight line. He speaks in bursts and pauses about the day it happened, on a stretch of rough shoreline during a rescue operation in a heavily wooded coastal area. What he can say with certainty is that another man was gravely injured in an accident Harjit believes he set in motion. When he tries to recount it deliberately, the story breaks apart. He can offer a flash of wet rock under his boots, the sharp smell of salt and pine, the scream of metal under strain, a body falling in a way that still makes his stomach drop. Then there is a gap. When he pushes himself to remember more, he says it is as if the memory goes dead on him. But at other times it returns all at once, with a force that feels present rather than past: the blare of emergency sirens, the cold air off the water, the color of the trees, the impact in his chest when he realized someone had been badly hurt.

In the weeks after the accident, Harjit told himself it had not happened the way he feared, or at least not as badly. He would correct his own mind when it drifted toward the scene, insisting he should think about the good that came after, the people who survived, the fact that worse outcomes were possible. He has spent years trying to replace intrusive fragments with forced gratitude and “positive thoughts,” as he puts it. If an image surfaced, he shoved it away. He came to believe that dwelling on it was dangerous, that if he let the full picture form he might not be able to contain it. Yet this effort has left the event in his mind as disconnected pieces rather than a settled memory, and when it breaks through it does so with a vividness that overwhelms him.

What has stayed most powerfully in his daily life is the sense that he must remain on guard. Harjit watches entrances, windows, the movements of other people. In any waiting room, restaurant, temple function, or family gathering, he chooses his seat carefully, preferring a wall behind him and a clear path out. He does not describe this as habit so much as necessity. He says he cannot relax unless he knows where danger could come from and how he would respond. Unfamiliar places trouble him especially. If he cannot quickly understand the layout, he feels exposed and unsettled, and over time he has narrowed where he is willing to go.

Natural settings have become particularly difficult. A park with dense trees, the smell of damp earth, a rocky waterfront, even certain stretches of highway where the landscape opens into brush and shoreline can stop him cold. For a man whose Coast Guard life once tied him to the outdoors, this has been a painful constriction. He still remains connected to that world, but he avoids settings that resemble the scene of the accident whenever he can. If he has to pass through such a place, he becomes tense and watchful, as if something terrible could happen again at any moment. Sirens are another immediate rupture. Hearing them from a passing ambulance or patrol vehicle can bring the whole scene back with crushing sensory force, and afterward he may sit in silence for hours, unable to explain to anyone what just happened inside him.

Talking about the future is unexpectedly difficult for him as well. When relatives ask about plans, or former colleagues talk about upcoming events, Harjit becomes withdrawn. He does not say much, but the conversation seems to catch on something painful. He has come to feel that there is something fundamentally wrong with him, that the accident revealed the kind of man he really is. He speaks of it not as a terrible mistake but as evidence of defective character. In his mind, what happened fits with “the sort of person” he is, and that belief carries a heavy shame.

There have also been periods when, instead of pulling back, he has taken needless risks. He is matter-of-fact about this, as if courting harm made a grim kind of sense. Those moments sit alongside his caution, both part of how he has lived since the accident. His family has noticed the changes most in his narrowing routines, his reluctance to go somewhere new, his scanning of every room, and the way certain sounds or landscapes can make him disappear into himself.

Now, after years of trying to master the memories by dismissing them, outrunning them, or covering them with forced optimism, Harjit has sought help because the effort is no longer working. He says he is tired of being startled by sirens, tired of declining invitations because he does not know the place, tired of feeling that a simple conversation about next month or next year can leave him shaken. What frightens him most is the possibility that the accident says something final about who he is. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is to be able to remember what happened without feeling as if he is back there again, and to sit in the world with a little less vigilance.
